name: Painted Grey Ware culture
title: The story of the Painted Grey Ware culture

text: About 3,200 years ago, people in northern India made fine grey pots painted in black, which give their culture its name.
These cups and bowls were precious, and were used mostly for drinking.
src: a fine, grey pottery painted with geometric patterns in black / conventionally dated c. 1200 to 600–500 BCE / found at 1,576 sites in northern India / an archaeologists’ name, taken from its most distinctive find
The painted grey ware was a luxury: almost all of it is drinking ware

text: They lived on the plain of the Ganges River, mostly in small farming villages.
Their houses were made of mud, brick, or woven sticks covered with clay.
src: It belongs to the Iron Age of the western Gangetic plain / Most PGW sites were small farming villages
Houses were built of wattle and daub, mud or brick

text: Farmers used the plough to grow rice, wheat, millet and barley.
They kept cattle, sheep, pigs and horses.
src: People grew rice, wheat, millet and barley, using the plough
kept cattle, sheep, pigs and horses

text: They are thought to have brought the skill of working iron to these plains.
src: the groups who made the pottery are thought to have brought iron technology to the Indo-Gangetic plains

text: Some villages grew into towns, with walls of earth, paved streets and ornaments of gold and ivory.
They probably lived in the time of the Kuru kingdom, when the holy Vedic texts were put in order.
src: The largest were fortified with ditches or moats and embankments of piled earth / with ornaments of gold, copper, ivory and semi-precious stones / paved streets
It probably corresponds to the middle and late Vedic period and the Kuru-Panchala kingdom / The Kuru kingdom, with which it is associated, systematised the Vedic religious literature

text: Later, many of their villages and towns grew into the cities of a new age.
Today archaeologists know more than 1,500 of their sites.
src: many PGW settlements grew into the large towns and cities of the Northern Black Polished Ware period
2018: 1,576 Painted Grey Ware sites are known
